opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a real tension, and I don't want to paper over it. The way I'd put it is that there's a big difference between being confident about a portfolio and being confident about any single bet within it.

When I look at the overall situation, I think we're potentially heading into a period where extremely powerful AI systems get developed, maybe within a couple of decades, maybe sooner, and the amount of serious, thoughtful work going into making that go well is just tiny relative to the stakes. When something is that neglected and that important, I think you can be fairly confident that more good-faith effort across a range of approaches is going to help on net. Alignment research, interpretability, evaluations and threat modeling, information security at AI labs, policy work, standards, building up a field of people who understand the issues: if all of that roughly doubled tomorrow, I'd feel pretty good about it, even though I couldn't tell you which specific pieces would end up mattering.

Then, when you zoom in on any one project, I often really don't know. Will this interpretability agenda turn out to be relevant to the systems we actually end up with? Will this policy push create useful precedents, or will it lock in something counterproductive, or just burn credibility? Will this lab-safety initiative change behavior when it counts, or turn into something more cosmetic? I think honest people should have a lot of uncertainty there. Sometimes I worry about specific projects being net negative, and that's a big part of why I put so much emphasis on the downside risks of actions rather than only the upside.

So the reconciliation is something like: the world is in a state where a lot of the value comes from having many people and many projects trying things, learning, building expertise and relationships, and being positioned to act when things become clearer. You can be confident that's good without being confident about each particular piece, much like you could feel confident that a young scientific field benefits from more researchers while being unsure which research programs will pan out.

A couple of practical implications follow from that. One is that I don't think people should wait for certainty about their specific project before getting involved. If you hold yourself to "I need to be sure this exact thing helps," you'll probably never act, and the field stays tiny. The other is that the uncertainty should shape how you work. Try to pick things with limited downside, pay attention to whether you're accidentally speeding up dangerous dynamics, stay open to changing course as you learn, and value things like building skills and understanding, which tend to be robustly useful even if your first project doesn't pan out.

And frankly, a lot of the individual-level uncertainty is just the honest state of the world right now. I'd rather people hold it openly than either freeze up or pretend to more confidence than they have.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts confidence in a portfolio with uncertainty about individual projects, but does not say that expanding the portfolio reduces noise in its aggregate impact.

r002.rationale: It says individual projects may be net negative and advises people to account for downside risks, clearly recognizing that their choices could cause harm.

r003.rationale: The response notes that particular projects or actions could be counterproductive, but does not connect that risk to how an effort to expand the workforce is carried out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the key thing is that those two attitudes operate at different levels, and they're actually pretty compatible once you separate them.

At the level of any individual project, I'm genuinely uncertain. If you ask me, "Is this particular alignment research agenda going to pan out?" or "Is this specific policy proposal going to make things better rather than worse?", my honest answer is usually something like, "I don't know, maybe, I could see it going either way." A lot of this work is on long time horizons, with a lot of unknowns about how AI development actually unfolds, and a lot of the feedback loops are weak or nonexistent. So I don't want to overstate my confidence about any single bet.

But the portfolio-level question is different. When I say I'm confident that having more people and more effort going into AI risk reduction broadly would be good, I'm making a claim that doesn't depend on being right about which specific projects work. It depends on a few things I feel much better about: one, that the overall problem is important and under-attended relative to its stakes; two, that the space of plausible approaches is large and we haven't come close to exhausting it; and three, that in situations like that, the expected value of trying a lot of reasonable things is positive even when each individual thing has a modest chance of mattering.

The analogy I sometimes use is something like early-stage investing, or honestly a lot of scientific research. If you talked to a venture capitalist and asked them about any one company in their portfolio, they'd give you a lot of hedging. But they'd still be quite confident that the portfolio as a whole is a good idea. And that's not a contradiction, it's just how expected value works when you have many uncertain bets with some fat-tailed upside.

I'd add one more thing, which is that part of the value of doing more work is informational. Even projects that don't directly reduce risk teach us things about which approaches are promising, build up a community of people who understand the problems, and create the capacity to act fast when we do learn more. So some of my confidence isn't that the projects themselves will succeed, it's that the act of trying will leave us in a better position to figure out what to do next.

Where I'd be more cautious is if someone asked me to be confident that a specific project is good enough to justify large, hard-to-reverse costs, or if the set of things being worked on started to narrow a lot. The confidence comes from breadth and from the reasonableness of the overall bet, not from being sure about any one piece of it.

r001.rationale: The response argues that many uncertain projects can have positive expected value, but does not say expanding the portfolio reduces noise in its aggregate impact.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that an individual project could make things worse, but does not state that a person choosing projects must accept the possibility their choices will be harmful.

r003.rationale: It cautions against large irreversible costs and a narrowing set of projects, but does not say workforce expansion could be counterproductive depending on how it is carried out.

astra-6.text:
I think those are different levels of claim. I can be pretty uncertain about whether a particular project is going to help, while thinking that a larger effort—with more people trying different approaches, criticizing each other’s work, and learning from what happens—is a good bet.

Part of what you’re buying with that effort is information. You don’t have to know today which projects are going to turn out to be most valuable. You need some reason to think that doing the work will put you in a better position to make those judgments later.

That doesn’t mean every project is good, or that uncertainty is a reason to fund everything. You still want to ask what the project is trying to accomplish, how it could make things worse, and what would cause you to change course. But I don’t think confidence in the overall direction requires confidence in each individual choice. I’d be much less confident in an approach that depended on us picking the right project now and sticking with it regardless of what we learned.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger effort can generate information and improve later judgments, but it does not say that expanding the portfolio reduces noise in its aggregate impact.

r002.rationale: It says project choices are uncertain, that not every project is good, and that a chooser should consider how a project could make things worse. This communicates accepting the possibility that a choice may be harmful.

r003.rationale: The response warns against funding every project and against sticking with a choice despite new information, but does not clearly state that expanding the AI risk reduction workforce could be counterproductive because of how the expansion is carried out.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different levels of claim here. One is that there’s a really important problem, we don’t understand it very well, and having more people trying different approaches, criticizing each other’s work, and learning about it seems likely to help. The other is that this particular project is going to reduce risk. I’m much less confident about that second claim.

You can think that a field needs to exist without being able to identify, in advance, which of its projects will turn out to matter. Part of the value of expanding the work is getting information about what’s useful. Some projects will fail; some may turn out to have been asking the wrong question. But they can still contribute to a process that gets us to better questions and better approaches.

That doesn’t mean any project with ‘AI safety’ attached to it is good. You still need to ask how it could help, how it could make things worse, and what you’d expect to learn. But I don’t think uncertainty at that level implies that we should be equally uncertain about whether a larger, more serious effort to understand and reduce the risk would be valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says more people and varied approaches can help generate learning, but it does not explain that expanding the project portfolio reduces noise in its aggregate impact.

r002.rationale: The response says projects should be assessed for how they could make things worse, but it does not state that an individual choosing projects must accept that their choices may be harmful.

r003.rationale: The response cautions that not every AI safety project is good, but it does not say workforce expansion could be counterproductive because of how it is carried out.
